argumentative_quality.premise_acceptability: Moderate - relies on contested philosophical premises (e.g., digital access as primary good, no-exit as coercion, algorithmic opacity as arbitrary power)

Due process mandates may dictate editorial judgment

philosophical_orientation.sentiment: Egalitarian liberal with republican and deliberative elements

structural_organization.structure_type: Four numbered sections plus introduction and conclusion; each section builds on the previous

summary_of_core_decisions: The essay argues that digital platforms are quasi-public actors because network effects eliminate exit, making consent illusory and enabling arbitrary algorithmic power. It uses Rawls to defeat Nozick's property defense, Nissenbaum to defeat consent, and Pettit to establish non-domination as the relevant freedom. It then resolves the expressive freedom objection by distinguishing substantive speech from procedural transparency, allowing public law to mandate accountability without dictating content.

thesis_commitment.hedging_density_in_final_paragraph: Low - final paragraph is assertive and programmatic
